title: Tuning the universality class of a quantum process by Trotterization
authors: Robin Prampain dit Boulan, Jerom Jebai, Hendrik Weimer
abstract: We numerically analyze a discretized version of the quantum contact process, a non-equilibrium model having a competition between a coherent infection process and a dissipative recovery process. Previously, the continuous-time version has been discussed to have a phase transition in a novel quantum universality class, while experimental investigations of a related process have pointed towards the transition being in the classical directed percolation class. We demonstrate that these differences stem from details of the discretization of the process and construct a systematic way to continuously interpolate between these results. Finally, we provide evidence that the modification of the universality class is due to destructive interference effects, showing a clear quantum-mechanical origin.
summary: The authors investigate the quantum contact process to resolve a conflict over its critical universality class. They demonstrate that the observed difference between theoretical and experimental predictions stems from the details of the Trotterization discretization used in simulations. By systematically tuning this discretization, they construct a continuous interpolation path connecting the two predicted classes.
main_problem: The paper resolves a controversy regarding the universality class of the quantum contact process (QCP) phase transition, which was debated between a novel quantum class and the classical directed percolation (DP) class.
main_result: The discrepancy in critical exponents is shown to arise from the details of the Trotterization discretization; by systematically tuning the discretization parameters, a continuous path connecting the QCP and DP universality classes is established.
method: Numerical analysis using Matrix Product State (MPS) simulations on a 1D lattice to calculate the effective critical exponent ($\delta_{eff}$) across different parameter regimes.
model_or_system: The quantum contact process (QCP) on a 1D lattice, modeled by a Lindblad master equation involving coherent infection dynamics ($H$) and dissipative recovery processes. The dynamics are analyzed after discretization via the Suzuki-Trotter expansion.
key_observables: Effective critical exponent ($\delta_{eff}$), which characterizes the long-time decay of average density $\langle n(t) angle$; a diagnostic ratio $R(t)$ comparing dark-to-bright state probabilities.
important_parameters: The ratio governing dynamics ($\Omega/\gamma$), and the discretization angles ($	heta$ for coherent, $\phi$ for dissipative), which are tuned to interpolate between regimes.
main_assumptions: The primary approximation is the use of a first-order Suzuki-Trotter expansion to discretize the continuous-time quantum evolution.
figures_summary: Implied figures show the effective critical exponent ($\delta_{eff}$) smoothly varying as a function of the dissipation angle $\phi$, demonstrating convergence from the QCP value towards the DP value. A ratio $R(t)$ is shown to distinguish between the two regimes.
paper_structure: The paper first sets up the continuous-time model and then analyzes its discretized version using Trotterization. The core of the work involves systematically varying the discretization parameters ($\phi$) to map out a continuous interpolation path between known critical behaviors (QCP vs DP).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles non-equilibrium phase transitions in quantum systems, providing quantitative evidence that the choice of numerical simulation method can fundamentally alter predicted universal physics.

FIG. 2. Discrete dynamics of a single timestep for L = 2. System qubits si are coupled to an ancilla qubit a initialized in |0⟩. The coherent dynamics is performed via Controlled-Rx rotation gates on the system qubits with the coherent angle θ. The dissipative step is performed by coupling each system qubit to the corresponding ancilla using a parametric swap (Rxy) gate with the dissipative angle ϕ. Finally, the ancilla is reset to |0⟩, providing a dissipative element.

FIG. 3. Effective critical exponent of the Trotterized contact process. (a) In the long-time limit, δeff(t) approaches the QCP value of 0.36 for a small Trotter angle θ = 3π/32 (L = 60). (b) For larger values of θ, the critical exponent δ according to the long-time limit continuously drops from the QCP value towards the DP value of 0.159 (dashed lines). The behavior is consistent for different system sizes, ruling out strong finite-size effects. Error bars are standard errors from bootstrapping with 100 samples.

FIG. 4. Emergence of dark states. (a) Strong coherent in- fection coupling Ωonly couples the bright states. Weak dis- sipation γ can trap the system in a dark state, in which no infections are possible until the next dissipative event. (b) Ratio R(t) between dark and bright state pairs at critical- ity, showing a clear difference between the continuous-time case belonging to the QCP universality class and θ = 3π/4 belonging to the DP universality class. Error bars denote represenative Monte-Carlo sampling errors. The inset shows that the drop from R(t →∞) ≈2 occurs around the θ value where the universality class starts to deviate from QCP.
